title: Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Boston College (Carroll School of Mgmt) - November 7, 2019
summary: Pabrai walks a Boston College class through GrafTech as a live 'IPSCO 2.0' case (captive low-cost needle coke, five-year cash flows roughly equal to market cap, Brookfield as capital allocator), then confesses his struggle to pay up for and hold on to compounders like Moutai and Ferrari. He also covers Munger's 'learn from mistakes but not too much' phone call, judging managers by track record (Marchionne, Tavares, Motherson Sumi), bulletproof businesses in Turkey and South Korea, owner earnings, and staying within a tiny circle of competence.

ideas.idea: Discussing a current position like GrafTech avoids the selection bias of only teaching past home runs, and even the best analyst is wrong one in three times.
ideas.detail: He picks GrafTech because the valuation is near his purchase price and the facts are current; quotes John Templeton that investing is a game of probabilities, and cites Johnson & Johnson talc and PG&E as examples of unpredictable trajectories, which is why you own a few businesses rather than one or two.

ideas.idea: IPSCO was third-grade math: $15/share cash plus $30/share of contracted cash flow over two years exceeded a stock price in the forties, so all the plants and know-how came free.
ideas.detail: Around 2003-04 the tubular steel maker had no debt, confirmed backlog with locked margins, and even though earnings could go to zero or negative after two years the risk-reward was very favorable.

ideas.idea: GrafTech's edge is captive, hedged needle coke at about $2,750/ton versus $4,500-7,000/ton for competitors, so its next five years of cash flow roughly equal its market cap.
ideas.detail: Of ~180-190k tons of UHP electrode capacity, ~145k tons carry the low-cost advantage; selling near $10,000/ton yields north of $1 billion in margin, and after ~$300 million of overhead, capex and debt service plus taxes, $500-600 million a year is locked in for several years.

ideas.idea: The needle coke tightness could run well beyond five years because no non-China plant has been built in ~40 years, a new one takes ~7 years and several hundred million dollars, and EV batteries compete for the same coke.
ideas.detail: Only four needle coke producers exist outside China (two US, two Japan); the know-how to build plants is nearly gone and no non-China player has announced capacity, so the seven-year clock keeps rolling forward.

ideas.idea: Owning a business alongside a prudent capital allocator like Brookfield, which owns 80% and understands buybacks, means excess cash flow will likely be returned efficiently.
ideas.detail: Three Brookfield people sit on the GrafTech board; Brookfield also cut six plants to three and drove manufacturing efficiencies, and the company is moving work from Monterrey to Pennsylvania to lower costs further.

ideas.idea: Heads I win, tails I don't lose much: downside protection is fundamental to every investment, per Buffett's rule number one.
ideas.detail: With GrafTech the floor is covered and the upside is hard to gauge; with Fiat Chrysler in 2012 you got all of Chrysler (Jeep, RAM) for free plus a hidden advantage in the 2009 UAW contract signed in 20 minutes under Auto Task Force pressure, which made Detroit one of the cheapest places on the planet to build a car.

ideas.idea: Ideally what we want is long-term compounders with huge runways and a flywheel that is hard to penetrate, like Costco possibly dwarfing its US footprint with China.
ideas.detail: Costco's first China store got mobbed; it is only in a handful of countries today, so the model has decades of possible rollout, though outcomes remain uncertain.

ideas.idea: As a cheapskate at the core, my unwillingness to pay up for great businesses is a huge disadvantage, and paying up for huge-runway compounders is probably worth it.
ideas.detail: Munger told him the failed Costco-Walmart merger terms would not have mattered because the pie would have been so much larger; Costco doesn't look cheap today but could be very cheap on a 20-year view. He names two lessons he has yet to learn: paying up and holding on.

ideas.idea: I should never, ever have sold Moutai: bought under 150 RMB four or five years ago, sold at an average of 800-900, and it now trades around 1,200.
ideas.detail: He calls Moutai the deepest moat on the planet, a thousand-year-old brand entrenched in over a billion minds that, unlike Costco, does not have to execute brilliantly every day; he captured 5-6x but was fully out before 1,000.

ideas.idea: Guy Spier is light years ahead of me at holding: his untouched 2012 Fiat Chrysler bet plus gifted Ferrari shares turned $10 million into roughly $70 million, while I sold Ferrari at $50-120 thinking it was fully priced.
ideas.detail: Guy bought 2 million shares at ~$5 (a 5% bet of a ~$200 million fund) and received 200,000 Ferrari shares now worth ~$165 each (~$33 million); Pabrai bought ~12 million shares as a 10% bet, made ~$100 million on Ferrari, but would have had ~$220 million had he held. Ferrari has never spent a dollar on advertising in 70-plus years.

ideas.idea: My aspiration is to buy Moutai at a PE of one and still hold it at a PE of 100 when earnings have grown 20-30x; I am trying again with Micron, which I think is a misunderstood compounder.
ideas.detail: He says God keeps giving him compounders (Moutai, Ferrari) that he is too dumb to keep, and this time he will try to hold even at four or five times the current value, though holding is very hard for him.

ideas.idea: A tiny circle of competence is enough to get extremely wealthy; you can trade IQ points for patience and stick-to-your-circle genes.
ideas.detail: Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire developing real estate only within five miles of Stanford, buying when vacancies were high and selling at low cap rates, passing on 99.999% of great investments. Envy of the idiot neighbor making money is detrimental to financial health.

ideas.idea: Unlike Buffett's Swiss Army knife, most investors have only one to three tricks, and one trick is more than enough.
ideas.detail: Buffett's breadth of experience lets Berkshire do deals like the $10 billion Occidental financing at 8% with warrants, like 2009; ordinary investors may never develop that range and don't need to.

ideas.idea: You can be a successful part-time investor with a passionate non-investing career; being comatose on trading and finding roughly one idea a year is enough.
ideas.detail: He spent 15-20 hours a week on investing while running his IT company; his radiation oncologist college roommate makes ~$1 million a year but his investing wealth dwarfs it, so oncology is now 'a hobby'.

ideas.idea: Learn from your mistakes but don't learn too much; you have to move on quickly, as Munger told me in his only phone call to me after I overanalyzed Horsehead in my letters.
ideas.detail: Horsehead Holdings, a zinc processor, went to zero after a large gain. Munger's concern was that dwelling on it would mess with his mind; Guy Spier got so absorbed in the Horsehead bankruptcy committee that he couldn't hear Pabrai pitching Moutai and only bought ~$100,000 of it.

ideas.idea: Even Buffett makes lots of mistakes: equal-weighted, Berkshire's acquisitions have a poor record, but dollar-weighted he was right on the big ones.
ideas.detail: Wedgewood Partners' letter listed IBM, Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, not enough Apple, and missing Microsoft and Google; nearly all Berkshire retail investments other than Borsheims and Nebraska Furniture Mart failed. Mistakes are par for the course.

ideas.idea: Almost every company in existence today will eventually be a zero; creative destruction means almost no business survives 30-50 years, let alone 100.
ideas.detail: The Good to Great companies mostly faltered; GE is about the only hundred-year compounder and look where it is; GEICO was on its knees in the 1970s. He can bet Moutai survives 50 years but is unsure about Costco or MasterCard, which is another reason to own more than one stock.

ideas.idea: Don't trust projections; judge managers by long track records, and rockstar executors like Marchionne, Tavares, Mittal and Sehgal keep making it work.
ideas.detail: Marchionne had an eight-year auto record and Harvard cases before 2012, having fixed a Fiat losing $100-150 million a month; Carlos Tavares turned GM Europe profitable (north of $1 billion a year) in nine months after GM lost money there for 20 years; Ajay Banga's Citibank record preceded MasterCard.

ideas.idea: Motherson Sumi's flywheel is getting paid by OEMs to take over distressed suppliers, compounding at 30% a year for 25-30 years in the auto parts business.
ideas.detail: They never solicit or answer acquisition calls; only when an OEM like BMW asks them to rescue a loss-making mirror supplier do they act, receive $50-75 million to take it over, never relocate plants to China, replace the top executive with a young insider, and turn it profitable within about six months.

ideas.idea: Look for Jim Collins' level-five leader traits: ambitious for the organization, not themselves, low ego and servant leadership, and avoid Chainsaw Al types.
ideas.detail: Tavares wears off-the-rack suits, flies coach while peers use private jets, and buys his own deli sandwich when visiting plants; Al Dunlap at Sunbeam blew up spectacularly. Philip Fisher's book also lists traits of great leaders.

ideas.idea: In countries with deteriorating institutions or crazy inflation, own bulletproof businesses that transcend geography and currency, like the Coke bottler or the dominant credit rating agency.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Growing up in socialist India, the Coke bottler still did fine; people will trade a certain amount of labor for a Coke even if the currency is seashells. In Turkey he told his Graham-overdosed local friend to skip the PE-of-0.1 stocks and visit the Coke bottlers, where paying three times earnings is fine.

ideas.idea: Don't focus on discounted pies; what you really want are growing pies, and South Korea offers more growing pies than Turkey.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: His single Turkish bet is a young entrepreneur with great assets bought at a ridiculous discount, but the whole pie was ~$40 million (probably worth north of $500 million) so he cannot deploy $100 million there. Korea's market has done nothing for three decades, governance is improving, the chaebols are losing power, and much more capital can be deployed there.

ideas.idea: Don't consciously try to expand your circle of competence; study businesses like HBS case studies and act only when seven moons line up and it is a no-brainer.
ideas.detail: He never reads anything on US healthcare, pharma or biotech because the sector is driven by non-market, corrupt forces; you can ignore 80-90% of the economy and still do well, but it is worth understanding Amazon and Google because so much flows through them.

ideas.idea: Ideas that go from 13 to 18 are not worth my time; I want at least a 3-5x, ideally 5x in five years, though 5x in ten years is fine.
ideas.detail: He reviews portfolio companies at least quarterly since real change takes years, and triages incoming writeups in escalating steps of 10 minutes, then 30 minutes, then two hours; a natural gas pitch promising 80x was passed because it was a directional bet on prices.

ideas.idea: Look at owner earnings after capex; high capex is not a deal killer, and even the capex-heavy auto business gave a 4x in seven years on Fiat excluding Ferrari.
ideas.detail: The best businesses like MasterCard, Amazon and Google need no capex, and a Singapore friend refuses any capex business and does fine, but memory players have high capex alongside high owner earnings.
